Gastroenterology · published research

Intestinal injury (ischemia-reperfusion)

In one rat experiment, PBM did not protect the intestine and worsened histology at early time points, while measured lung injury decreased. Human evidence is absent.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In one rat experiment, PBM did not protect the intestine and worsened histology at early time points, while measured lung injury decreased. Human evidence is absent.

Summary of the Evidence

One direct publication tested low-level laser treatment in a rat model of intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury. Four related publications from the same broader research line examined lung changes after gut ischemia-reperfusion; those distant-organ outcomes should not be counted as evidence of intestinal healing, and overlap among the animal experiments cannot be ruled out. No human, in-vitro, or ex-vivo study of this indication was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No human PBM study for acute intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury was identified. The available evidence is a surgical rat model with acute tissue and distant-organ measurements.

Animal evidence

The direct study irradiated the serosal surface of the jejunum after ischemia and reperfusion. At 650 nm, in the red visible range, and 0.5 J/cm², intestinal histology was worse in treated animals at 0 and 1 hour after reperfusion; by six hours, the reported histology no longer differed. In contrast, lung injury was significantly lower in the laser-treatment groups. The organ-specific direction matters: the study found a distant lung effect without bowel protection at the tested settings (Kirkby et al. 2012).

Related experiments in the database also report reduced lung inflammation or oxidative injury after intestinal/gut ischemia-reperfusion. These are consistent with the possibility of a systemic or distant-organ response, but they do not overturn the direct intestinal result and should be interpreted as related outcomes rather than replication of bowel protection.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No direct cell-culture or isolated-tissue PBM experiment for this clinical indication was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The direct rat study used a 650-nm red visible laser at 70 mW and 0.5 J/cm², applied directly to the jejunal serosa after reperfusion. This requires operative exposure of the bowel and is not equivalent to external light delivery through abdominal skin. The experiment did not establish a beneficial intestinal dose or compare later treatment schedules.

Interpretation

At the tested dose and early time points, the bowel outcome was null or unfavorable, while lung injury decreased. Both findings should be retained rather than allowing the distant benefit to imply intestinal protection. A single acute animal experiment cannot determine whether another dose or timing would change the bowel response, and there is no human evidence.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for intestinal protection in acute rat ischemia-reperfusion injury Very low for reduced remote lung injury in the same model
Publications and records5 relevant articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One rat experiment found that 650-nm light worsened early intestinal histology or made no difference by six hours, while lung injury decreased in treated groups. The opposite organ-specific directions are important and have not been independently repeated. Further studies should vary dose and treatment timing and measure bowel and lung outcomes separately before translation is considered.
